title: Why The Ordinary, Everyday, And Mundane Is Key To Good Behavior And Academic Improvement
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that teachers who focus only on content, lessons, and academic performance while neglecting the ordinary, everyday details of running a classroom are making a fundamental mistake. He contends that the small, seemingly boring specifics—how students turn in work, transition between activities, or take out materials—have the greatest actual impact on behavior and success habits, because excellence is built through consistent insistence on doing everything a certain way. He clarifies that this precision doesn't require rigidity or militaristic control; his own students, he notes, walk across campus as a loose, happy group rather than a strict line, because clear expectations and consistent accountability underlie the apparent casualness. The article frames sustained focus on mundane details as the underappreciated key to inspiring pride, boosting morale, and improving both behavior and academic performance.
points: Focusing primarily on content and academics while neglecting mundane classroom details is identified as a common teacher mistake.
Small, seemingly boring specifics—how work is turned in, how transitions happen—are said to have the greatest actual impact on behavior and success habits.
Precision and consistency in the mundane do not require rigidity; classrooms can remain relaxed and casual on the surface.
The teacher's own classroom is offered as an example: students walk in a loose, happy group rather than a strict line, underpinned by clear expectations.
Attention to ordinary, everyday details is framed as the most underutilized key to effective classroom management and academic improvement.
quotes: It’s only natural to want to focus on what matters. To concern yourself primarily with content, lessons, and academic performance.
The truth is, everything you do as a class affects how well your students behave and progress.

In fact, it’s the wee little boring details—like the way students turn in work or transition to a new activity or take out their laptops—that have the greatest impact on behavior, success habits, and the like.

Success is in the details” is as much or more true for teaching as any other profession. Yet, it’s the most underutilized and underappreciated key to effective classroom management and academic improvement.
Visitors to my own classroom are often surprised at my students’ sense of freedom and casualness. In fact, we often walk across campus not in a line, but in one silent but happy herd.
It’s the focus on what most teachers gloss over that is the secret to inspiring pride, boosting morale, improving behavior . . .
